Mr. T. L. CHURCH (North Toronto) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 7, to amend the Post Office Act.
He said: The object of this amendment is to provide for a uniform law, as in the United States, England and Australia, requiring swom semi-annual statements from all newspapers, magazines, trade journals and other periodicals which contain articles designed to influence public opinion, giving the names and addresses of editors, owners and stockholders. There is a proviso that this act shall not apply to religious, fraternal, temperance, scientific, or such other publications. The names of small stockholders are not required to be given. A copy of these sworn statements shall be published in such newspapers or other publications after they have been filed as required by the act. Any such publication which fails to comply with these provisions shall be denied admission to the mails. Paid editorials and other reading matter for which money is paid shall be plainly marked "Advertisement", as they properly should be. Statements under the act are to be made in duplicate and delivered to the Postmaster General, who shall make regulations for the carrying out of the provisions of the act. This legislation is introduced solely in the public interest and in the best interests of a free press and of the liberty of the press in a liberty-loving country. If the press is to serve the public more ade-28
quately in the future this legislation is not only a social but an economic necessity.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Agriculture-Fruit, including grant of $8,000 to the Canadian Horticultural Council, $200,000.

I do not want to hold up
the estimates unnecessarily, but here is a large item without any definite statement or detail as to what the money is to be used for. I also object to the increase of $18,000. I do not see why there should be any increase in this estimate. There is also an item of $S,000 for the Canadian Llorticultural Council. What are the functions of that council? What good do they do to the fruit industry or to the country?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
The first question is with regard to the increase. I may say that last year in a small way we took over a new service, which consisted of grading apples in the Okanagan valley, and issuing a certificate therefor. That was done on the request of 23i
the apple growers of British Columia, they offering to pay for the service. This service was only inaugurated with the Okanagan people to give us sufficient information, in order to show that a fee of $5 for inspecting a car and issuing the certificate would cover the cost of service. This $18,000 additional is for the purpose of extending the service to all the apple growers of Canada, in return for which we will charge a fee of $5, and the money will be recouped to the treasury. It was found that the old method of grading by the barrel was not as satisfactory nor as good for the industry as the government certificate would be.
With respect to the second question I may say the Horticultural Council was organized in Canada in 1922 and I think I could not do better than just read the report of the council to the House. The report says:
To advance all matters tending towards the improvement of the horticultural and allied industries in Canada, including plant origination and registration, production, grading, packing, transportation, storage and marketing;
(a)	Bj' bringing about a closer co-operation between those engaged in the horticultural and allied industries in Canada and a fuller understanding of their problems;
(b)	By initiating, fostering and assisting in obtaining such legislation and regulations as will be beneficial to the horticultui'al and allied industries;
Then as to the vegetable industry the report says:
(c)	By emphasizing through inter-provincial co-operation the importance of the horticultural and allied industries and to obtain for them the position they deserve as an important and progressive branch of agriculture;
And it goes on with a number of subdivisions; I do not think I need read the whole of them. The amount of grant each year was: In 1922 $5,000; 1923, SS.OOO; and so on. The reason the addition was made to the grant was the new work they took up in connection with the registration of new plants and new shrubs. That has been established for the first time in Canada, and I think for the first time on this continent: that is, issuing registration certificates for new breeds of plants and fruits, so that the originator of a new apple like the McIntosh or any other new variety of fruit could get a registration or pedigree, just as they obtain a pedigree for an animal. The report continues:
What the council has (a) undertaking is:
3. To bring about a closer co-operation between those engaged in the horticultural and allied industries in Canada and a greater understanding of their problems;
2.	The establishment of a plant registration bureau.
3.	The establishment of trial gardens.
4.	The establishment of demonstration gardens.
5.	The encouragement of horticultural research and production by means of medals, awards and diplomas.
Supply-Agriculture

There are a large number of others. This vote was included in the miscellaneous vote in former years, but this year it is attached to this particular branch.
Do we understand that the fees for grading apples will make this industry carry its own expense of grading?

No, just the new
grading. We have never officially graded apples or potatoes for shipment. It has always been done by the owner, and while that practice, which was introduced with the introduction of the Fruit Marks Act something like twenty years ago, has given great service, it is not altogether satisfactory. Consequently a species of government inspection on the car at the point of shipment was provided, to supervise the grading done by the owners, by opening the barrels and packages, to ascertain if they were graded correctly. If they are graded properly we issue a certificate to that effect. The issuing of that certificate by an impartial inspector gives additional value to the grades. The fee for that inspection is $5 a car.
Then this $18,000 is to make the initial payment for this service?
Yes.
And this will be returned in fees?	*

Yes, it will be
returned in the revenues of the country.
We understand this is only an advance to carry on the work and it will be returned in grading fees?

Yes. I may inform the committee that it cost us last year $11,000 to give the service in the Okanagan valley and the fee of $5 a car would amount to about $12,680. It was done in a place where it could be done more cheaply before, and it will cost more now.

If the results are the
same next year your revenue will be double the outlay, and you will be able to reduce the cost per car.

Well, it may work out that way. With reference to charging the fee, it is a question whether we should not do the same thing for a large number of inspectional services. With reference to the inspection of wheat by the grain inspectors at Winnipeg, it has always been the custom to charge in the old days 60 cents a car for small cars and 90 cents a car at the present time. We have not, except on some occasions like

this carried on the practice of charging for inspection or grading fees with regard to other farm products. We have the grading now of cheese and butter, and we have been discussing the wisdom of putting on a charge for grading butter and cheese, so much per box, two or three or four cents, and have this cover the cost of the service. We have discussed the wisdom of doing the same thing with regard to the grading of hogs. If the committee thinks that the time has arrived when these services are so well recognized, so valued and appreciated that we could very well charge a fee in the same way as we do for the inspection of wheat, I should be glad to hear what hon. members have to say regarding the matter.
As regards the inspection of fruits and vegetables, is it proposed to have an inspector supervise the grading?
No. The grading will be done exactly as before. A number of the receptacles will be opened in order that the inspector may find out whether the contents are up to grade and in good condition or not.

Will this iriake a complete change in the method of inspecting
apples?
No.
To what extent will there be a change?

It will be supplemental to the present grading. The grading will be exactly the same. Whether it is a carload at the port or point of shipment, we send a man in to inspect the fruit and find out its condition and whether it is graded properly. It will be an additional precaution.
Will this be done by the same inspector?
Yes.

The inspector will issue
a certificate?
Yes, a government certificate.
Is government inspection of these products to be made compulsory for goods consumed in Canada as well as goods for export?

This is entirely
optional. A request was made by the apple growers of-British Columbia. They felt that they could well afford to pay five dollars a car to get a government inspector's certificate,

Supply-Agriculture
so they made the proposal and offered to pay that amount of money. We thought we would try out this inspection in a small way last year. The proposal is to extend the service to any part of Canada where the people of that locality wish it to be applied. It will not be compulsory. Any part of Canada that wishes to get the old system of grading will be at liberty to do so.
Did this request come from the shippers or the growers?
From both.
Does the inspection apply to potatoes as well as fruit?
Yes, I understand the same request has been made with regard to the shipment of potatoes.
From the growers?
Yes.
What potato growers?
In British Columbia.
How many additional inspectors does the minister expect this will mean?

That will depend upon how many people take advantage of the service. It will probably mean from ten to fifteen inspectors. We had eleven last year. If the Niagara peninsula and the Annapolis valley both request a similar service, probably fifteen additional inspectors will be required.
That will be for the fruit. Supposing this service is extended to vegetables, for instance potatoes?
That will take still more. The Ashcroft potato growers and others in British Columbia made the same request and we acceded to it on the same terms.

The minister has men who look after seed, feed and fertilizer control, and a great deal of that work comes at a different season of the year from the grading of fruit and vegetables. Would it not be possible to use the same staff on the two different branches of work instead of adding to the departmental staff for this purpose? It has been suggested to me that especially the seed inspection is a seasonal occupation that may occupy only a short part of the winter season, and owing to the fact that there is no continuous occupation for these men, the same men do not come back next year and a new crop of men is taken on. My
opinion is that if the same men could be employed in the other branches of inspection work the minister would be able to retain those men through the season, have the advantage of any experience they had in past years and ensure much better results than would be possible with a new force of men taken on each year.

That request on
the face of it is reasonable enough. As regards the Seed branch, that will come before the committee in a little while. A Sufficient number of new activities have been taken on by the Seed branch during recent years to occupy the whole of their time. The Feeding Stuffs Act has necessitated more time and men; but even since then, the act with respect to the grading of hay was taken over recently from the Department of Trade and Commerce and the act with respect to the inspection of hides and fertilizers has been taken over as well. All these additional services have been taken on by the Seed branch and -they keep the time of the staff entirely occupied. The work of the great majority of the fruit inspectors, except possibly the port inspectors, is of a seasonal nature, four or five months.
Does the shipper or the buyer pay the charge of five dollars for the inspection of a carload of apples or other fruit?

Whoever asks for
the service pays for it.

The minister says that the inspector issues a certificate. Provided that the inspector issues a certificate that the fruit is in first class condition and deterioration sets in from any cause after a few weeks have elapsed in transportation, will the buyer be forced to accept the oar on that certificate? I presume that is the intention.
We are giving the same service, no matter who asks for it. If there is any objection on the part of the buyer to the grading after the certificate is issued, we will give a re-inspection.
Where?

At the point of
delivery.
Then it is optional whether a car is inspected or not.
Yes.

I think the minister should go further and inspect every carload before it leaves the shipping point.
Supply-Agriculture

Was the total number
of inspectors in Nova Scotia reduced last season, and if so by how many, and why?

WTe thought that
by making them work a little harder, cover a little bit more ground, maybe go on duty a week or two earlier and maybe stay on a week longer, a smaller number of the best men would be able to cover the work. As these activities increase in volume and number, the number of our staff is necessarily increased, and in our desire to keep that down to the minimum consistent with service, we cut some of them out. The taking on of this additional service will, of course, necessitate additional inspectors, but this expense will be paid out of the revenue that we derive from the charge of five dollars a car.

If a car of apples is ordered
and inspected and a certificate is given, has that certificate any binding effect so far as the purchaser is concerned in the event of the consignment proving on delivery to be not in accordance with the specification?

The system is merely a means of facilitating business between buyer and seller. The same question came up the other day in connection with the grading of dairy products and it has also arisen in the case of the grading of grain. I do not know of any system of inspection under which the government holds itself responsible for the consequences of its grading certificates.
Mr. BOY'S:	The minister misunderstands
me; I do not suggest that the government would be responsible. If the certificate had a binding effect as between the two parties to the contract I could appreciate the fact that it would be far-reaching and useful. But so far as I know, it has no legal effect; it does not preclude the purchaser from rejecting the stock, whatever it may be. If, however, there is such a provision I should like to know where to find it.

Invariably, where
there is a system of grading provided by law, the certificate is accepted by buyer and seller, but I am not sufficiently versed in the law to know whether such a certificate would hold in court. That, however, is the practice. If, for instance, a car of potatoes is graded at point of shipment in the Maritime provinces, the purchaser being in Montreal, let us say, the consignment might be refused on the ground that the grading was too high. An inspector of the department would then be called in and would re-inspect the shipment, and the decision is usually accepted by the

buyer in such transactions. I do not know, however, what force the certificate would have in law, although in my experience the arrangement has always been satisfactory to both buyer and seller. Indeed, both .parties have always seemed to be so satisfied that new services of this kind are constantly being asked for. That is the reason for the present service. Last year, I might mention in illustration, several carloads of turkeys arrived from western Canada for Toronto and Montreal, the draft being attached to the bill of lading in the usual way. The buyers refused to take delivery on the ground that the shipment was not properly graded; the poultry, it appeared, was not dressed. There was no system of grading for dressed poultry; it was merely a matter of sending representatives to the siding to superintend the transportation of the consignment. It was cold weather, the birds got frozen, and their value was reduced. Finally by negotiation and adjustment an agreement was arrived at, but owing to the fact that there was no federal grading system some difficulty was experienced. The public are always running up against such difficulties and that is why they are asking for grading in order to facilitate business and reduce friction to the minimum.

If the certificate were made
binding by statute it would prevent a great deal of litigation which now goes on. If inspection were asked for by vendor and purchaser at point of shipment, the goods being sold f.o.b., and if the certificate being once given were in law binding on the parties, it would be of great service to the people. Without some such provision, however, it seems to me that very little good results; at the very most I suppose you provide a witness who may be called at the trial of the dispute and who, of course, by virtue of his office, would be an independent witness whose word would have weight with the judge. Beyond that I do not see what good results will accrue from the system without the element of binding force.

In my opinion, if
the purchaser of a carload of vegetables or of apples refused to accept the inspector's certificate, he would find that the case would go against him if he attempted to defend his action in a court of law.

Supposing that in the transportation of a carload of potatoes-the consignment got frozen: surely you do not suggest that the purchaser would be bound to accept that consignment, notwithstanding that a certificate might have been given?

Supply-Agriculture

I dc* not suggest
that. If the consignment was found to be unsatisfactory at point of delivery that information would be forwarded to the proper department and a re-inspection would ensue; and if the potatoes were frozen a report would be made accordingly and non-acceptance would be justified.
That, then, involves the question as to whether the contract is inspection on delivery, or f.o.b. The whole feature lies in that.

Re-inspection will
be available to anyone who demands it, and our experience is that the system has always worked satisfactorily.

Then your first certificate would not be of any effect. The question has been asked as to who pays for the inspection. Well, I think that is easily answered. The producer will pay for it eventually, because if there are two or three charges for inspection added to a cargo of goods, from the time it leaves the producer to the time it reaches the consumer, it is clear that a man will purchase cheaply enough to meet those charges. As a matter of fact, the purchaser does so, and that is right. My fear is that if you have two inspections on every carload, each of the parties will have to pay a five-dollar fee for the inspection and this will cut down the proceeds to the producer, which are already below cost of production, at any rate in the case of potatoes.
What about the consumer?

The price to the consumer is controlled by competition from other sources. If our potatoes are made to cost, through inspection, more than we can buy potatoes for from the United States, the minister can see what a disadvantage the local producer would be under. And I presume that the imports from the United States would' not be subject to the inspection. On that point it would be interesting to have some information.
Whoever asks for inspection gets it.
Would potatoes coming from the United States be subject to inspection?
Those coming in would be subject to grading, but in the case of our own product the system is purely optional; only those who ask for the service receive it.

I am aware that the number of inspectors in the Maritime provinces has been reduced during the past year. Was the same proportion of reduction made in Ontario and British Columbia last year as in the Maritime provinces?

Yes. We endeavour to divide the inspectors among the constituencies in the provinces on the basis of the number of barrels of apples exported. I can assure the hon. member that it is no easy matter to get down to mathematical exactitude, having regard to all the interests concerned. But the reduction was made uniformly.

For what reason was the inspectorial staff reduced and on whose advice was this reduction made? The province of Nova Scotia is a very important applegrowing centre, and this is becoming one of its great industries. The minister is proposing a system of certification and he wants to charge the producer of apples $5 on every car sent out. This will raise a riot among the fruit growers of the country. The inspection either is good or is no good, and it may be made at point of delivery or at the point where the apples are put on the train for transhipment. Nobody knows what is going to happen to these apples in transit; but if a man comes along with a government certificate that the apples were all right when shipped, then the vendee, who probably is defending an action on account of the goods not being in accordance with the guarantee, is non-suited. The sooner the minister gets away from endeavouring to put too many restrictions upon the fruit growers of this country, and the sooner he sees that adequate protection is given to our fruit growers the better it will be for all concerned.
Hear, hear.

I do not mean "adequate protection" in the sense understood by my right hon. friend; I mean adequate protection to the man who puts up an honest pack. That is all I am asking. The minister brings down legislation regarding which, I venture, to say he has consulted nobody but his officials at Ottawa. He has not gone through the province of Nova Scotia, for instance, and ascertained the views of the fruit growing people there. With a lot of high paid officials here he endeavours to force through the House legislation which is detrimental to the fruit growing industry of Nova Scotia. The first thing he should do is to decrease the number of his high paid officials an Ottawa instead of cutting down the number of inspectors in Nova Scotia. Every one of those
Supply-Agriculture

inspectors is a good man, I do not care who appointed him; each tries to do his duty. Last year he cut off an inspector in my constituency.
That is the trouble.

No, it is not my trouble. He can cut out the whole bunch so far as I am concerned. All I want to see is our people properly protected. The department cut off two inspectors in my hon. friend's (Mr. Robinson's) constituency in the county of Kings, where more apples are raised than in all the rest of Nova Scotia. Two more inspectors were cut off in Digby and Annapolis. The minister is not going to get a thorough inspection by discharging such good men. So long as there are apples to be shipped let the department keep a sufficient staff on hand so that the packers will not have to wait for inspection. To-day shipments are held up for lack of inspection. The minister says now that he is going to penalize the packer. Well, the average packer has faith in his pack, and he knows very weli that any failure on his part to keep his pack up to standard means that in the final analysis he will simply penalize himself. But the minister wants to have a big staff of pack inspectors to issue certificates to the packers, with the result that the vendee has no rights whatever in a court of law. Everybody knows the minister is talking against reason.
Order.

I say that without
hesitation. Every lawyer knows what he is up against in such cases.
Oh, oh.

It is all very well for
my hon. friends over yonder to laugh; they never saw an apple grown; and I venture to say that the hon. minister never saw an apple grown where he came from. Why does he not take the same 4 p.m. course as his colleagues would take in similar circumstances, consult the men who are to be affected by his proposals? If he does not want to take his friends on this side of the House intc his confidence, men who come from the apple-growing districts of Nova Scotia, let him get in touch with the apple growers themselves, instead of attempting to put legislation upon the statute book which is going to retard the apple growing industry of Nova Scotia. Let the minister come down to Nova Scotia, and we will show him that we can raise apples. We want proper inspection, we are not ashamed of the quality of our apples; but on account of a few men who do not agree on

what constitutes proper packing, do not let the minister take the advice of his officials in Ottawa, who do not know anything about apples, and then turn around and try to put restrictions upon the apple growing industry, of Nova Scotia.

The hon. member
for Hants (Mr. Martell) has touched a very important matter in connection with this item. I observe there is an increase of $18,000 over the estimate for last year, and an increase of $55,000 over that for 1921-2. What proportion of this vote is for the payment of officials and their expenses?

Mr. Chairman, I
suppose we have to give this information to every newcomer, and I will try to furnish it again as briefly as possible. This service is entirely optional; no part of Canada, whether it be the Annapolis valley, the Niagara peninsula or any other fruit growing district need accept it. The service was asked for in the Okanagan valley, we gave it last year, and we have found it self-supporting. I appreciate the grievance my hon. friend has brought to the attention of the committee; but 1 think that in justice to the grower of fruit in this country one simple basic principle ought to be remembered, and that is, that all fruit is perishable; it is not like iron or wood, that will last indefinitely. The variety of apples to which my hon. friend refers is what we call an early winter apple. I think about December is its main month of marketing. You cannot expect to keep a fall apple, for instance, a Transparent, through to Christmas. Another variety, the McIntosh, which comes along about October and into November cannot be kept over until March unless it is kept under ideal cold storage conditions, and then, once released from cold storage, it must be used immediately. The placing of creamery butter in cold storage may keep it in perfect condition, but once it is released, it must be used. The same applies to any article that is of a perishable character. It- is most unfair of the hon. member to suggest laying on the table a few selected specimens of apples and to say that these are a sample of what the Okanagan fruit grower sells or markets as No. 1 Fancy. The hon. member knows quite well that that is not the case. He, like anyone else, when he buys an article, is at liberty to use his eyes and to look the article over. I quite admit that if a retailer buys from a wholesaler a dozen boxes of apples, they are released from cold storage and he offers them for sale in his store. If he does not sell them for a few days, the

Supply-A gricul ture
very fact that they have been in cold storage and released will cause them immediately to commence deteriorating. If he keeps them in his store for a week, a month or two months-and probably these apples were in a store for six weeks or two months-naturally, they will deteriorate and they cannot be expected to maintain their perfection over a long period of time. No amount of inspection, no skill on the part of the inspector, no element of science in cold storage facilities, will ever rectify what my hon. friend is complaining of at this time. There is nothing that can be done in or out of this parliament, by scientists or others, that will change this condition; It is a condition of nature and nothing on earth can change it. I deprecate very much this suggestion being broadcasted throughout Canada in regard to the Okanagan fruit growers, a class of producers and horticulturists who have suffered perhaps as much as any other class of agriculturists in this country during the last thirty years in endeavouring to bring their products up to the highest degree of perfection possible. The result of their work is that this year the Okanagan fruit grower has, I think, time after time, taken first rank and first prize in international exhibition for his fruit.
While I am on this subject I should like to say a word in regard to some observations made by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell). I was in the Old Country last fall for a few months and I took particular care, for my information and satisfaction to look into the marketing of Canadian fruit. I saw a very large quantity of magnificent Nova Scotia apples marketed in England. I saw many of our own, and also a very large quantity of western American apples, that is apples from Washington and Oregon, Hood river and Wenatchee and so on, districts in the western states, offered for sale. The Canadian apples for sale on the London, Manchester, Sheffield and Liverpool markets in England did splendid credit to Canada. We are gradually building up a system of marketing these perishable goods at great distances and we ought to pause and realize what the grower is doing for himself, with the assistance certainly of the various governments, Dominion and provincial, through their officials. We ship scores of carloads of apples from the Okanagan Valley three hundred and fifty miles by rail to the Pacific coast, load them on steamers, ship them down through the tropical climate of the Panama canal, a month's journey or more, and unload them in England. And then they are distributed all over England, and distributed successfully, too. In a less circuitous way the Nova Scotians load their fruit on the
Atlantic and do a similar business. This is something which a few years ago was looked upon as a hopeless undertaking and yet it is done successfully to-day. And we are doing it by the aid of science and through the devoted attention and assiduous application of the growers, and the persistence of the producers generally, with such help as is given by the department. I say, therefore, that Canadian fruit is not represented in anything approaching a fair light by the remarks and the exhibits of my hon. friend.
Now, as to the protection of the consumer. Undoubtedly we ought to do all we can to protect the consumer, but I do not know what more we can do than we are doing. You will not do it by inspection, for if you inspect an article you examine it when it is packed, and you cannot expect that box to remain in the same condition from the time it leaves the producer until it is used by the consumer. Perhaps the consumer leaves it in his cellar or in a hot pantry, and apples that are treated in that way must fall to pieces through the very processes of nature. So that when anyone gets up and suggests that a fruit after going through these miscellaneous experiences should stand up like the perfect article he is not talking-well, I was going to say, common sense, but at any rate he is not saying what is reasonable.

In less than half a day apples that have been kept in cold storage will deteriorate when brought into a warm store. Yes, of course. As to size, a No. 1 apple, which is preferred by the very best hotels, our highest class of trade, is usually about the size of this specimen I have here. You can get a Wolf River apple almost as big as my hon. friend's head-not as big as he thinks it is but as big as it actually is; and you can get on the other hand a Northern Spy, which my hon. friends from Nova Scotia produce in such perfection, two or three times the size of this one. It is not reasonable, therefore, to produce a few culls, the brief history of which no one knows, and suggest that they are a reflection on the producers of fruit in this country.
Personally I do not know very much about the activities of this branch of the department, but I do know some of the inspectors; and speaking only of those with whose work I am acquainted, I must say that the department deserves credit. And if the department observes in all its inspectors the same high standard I have found in the case of those whom I know, I should have no complaint to make in regard to the inspection of fruit. As to the broad problem of how far we should extend the system of inspection while at the same time taking care to conserve the public rights in the way of taxation, this is a question of considerable importance. I rise now, however, merely for the purpose of repudiating, and repudiating strongly, the aspersion that was being broadcast by my hon. friend in regard to the producers of Okanagan whom I have known for the last thirty years and .vith whose struggles I am quite familiar.

Did the hon. member see the box out of which these apples were taken? I have never in my life seen a No. 1 like the specimen we have seen here and! I have seen many cars of apples that came out of British Columbia.

I may inform the hon. gentleman that the box from which these apples were taken is still in my cellar at home. I bought the apples as No. 1 Fancy Delicious, and hon. gentlemen will not wonder that I have brought the matter to the attention of the minister. The hon. member told us of the prizes which the British Columbia apple growers were able to win in the markets of the world. That is something we are all proud of. But what we would1 like would be to get some of these prize apples at home, and to know that we were getting good fruit when we paid $3.75 a box for apples. And that is what I paid for this particular lot. I bought them in the town of Nanton, sixty miles from Calgary.
I am not blaming the fruit growers of the Okanagan collectively for the condition of the apples I bought, I am simply bringing the matter to the attention of the minister; and when I do so I get a nice curtain lecture from the hon. member. Has he the interests of the apple growers at heart when he tries to make out that it is all right to label apples of this size and colour Fancy?
The hon. member has misrepresented' and misquoted me wholly and absolutely.

So far as that goes, I leave

I accept this sample as being a bona fide sample of the grade that my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) says it is. But might I point out the impossibility of checking up every parcel, whether box or barrel. The apples are packed by the growers or packers and graded by them. Our inspector does not inspect every box or every barrel; that would be impossible. He does not empty the apples out. He takes the head off the barrel, knocks down the hoop so as to loosen the staves, and sometimes he takes out a stave so as to get a sectional view of the contents, and from the information so obtained he has to judge about a dozen other barrels. As in eggs we inspect only one case in a dozen, so in apples we inspect only one barrel in about a dozen. Even with that inspection we require a considerable number of inspectors. I hear complaints that my department has too many inspectors, yet if we gave inspection of every parcel of apples we would need ten times as many men, and even then an apple such as that my hon. friend refers to might escape 24
detection. My hon. friends from the west will appreciate the fact that in spite of our inspection staff at Winnipeg and Fort William some cars of wheat get by that are
5 p.m. plugged with low grade wheat. If detected the whole carload is put at the lowest grade. Similarly with apples, when it is remembered that we inspect only one barrel out of twelve or fifteen, some inferior apples may get through. It only shows that if we had no inspection a much larger number of inferior apples would escape detection. When we had no Fruit Marks Act, I remember the quality of fruit sent into the west was terrible. A very marked improvement has taken place since, and we expect a still further improvement when the grower knows that he is going to be checked up more and more closely. Let me confirm the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) with respect to the quality of our apples. It is not on the inspection of one barrel or one apple that we are to judge of the quality of our apples. I can not only confirm the hon. member's statement, but I can go further, for according to the report brought back by my deputy, Canadian apples stand highest of any apples on the British market, showing that reasonable care is taken, not only b}' the men who grow the apples and pack them, but by the inspectors. I do not say that the system is perfect; you cannot get a perfect system of inspection as long as it is done by human means; even if every barrel were opened some odd apples of inferior quality would get past. The idea is, as has already been pointed out by one hon. member, to get such a system of inspection as will ensure to the buyer that he is getting the quality of apples described on the package and to get this inspection at (a reasonable expense.

It seems to me that the inspection should take place where the apples are grown and not at the seaboard. I see no economy in reducing the number of inspectors in a county like Hants, and putting on an inspector in the city of Halifax. I think such inspection is an unqualified joke. We find the estimates for this department are increased by $18,000. We find also another item of $24,000, which is really an increase, because the minister takes that sum off this estimate in expectation of getting it from the growers. As I said before, this minister is some little spender, and I think he had better get down to earth.

I have been charged with evading questions. I do not want to

If we are going
to give such inspection as will stop apples of the quality referred to by the hon. member for Macleod from coming through we will need ten times as many inspectors as we have to-day. The minister should keep up the inspectoral staff instead of cutting it down as he did last year, thus putting too much work on the inspectors who have to work morning, noon and night, because they have often to show the packers the requirements of the law. Surely the apple growers of this country are entitled to have every possible assistance from the department, and I am only asking the minister not to overwork his inspectors. We were satisfied with the staff which the department had in Nova Scotia two or three years ago, but unfortunately that staff has been cut down. Now the chief inspector of fruit in Nova Scotia should be located at or near Kentville in the county of Kings which is the centre of the fruit growing belt and is a county which produces more apples than the whole of the rest of the province put together. The chief inspector has been in his present location since the days of the Laurier government. I am not criticising the chief inspector personally, but there is no question that he should be situated where the inspectors from the other counties-Hants, Kings, Annapolis, Digby, Lunenburg-can conveniently meet him. Lunenburg, I may say, was not very much of a fruit growing county in the days gone by but is rapidly coming into its own in that respect. Last year the minister dropped five inspectors in Nova Scotia. That should not have been done. The result may have been to save $5,000, but the consumer as well as the fruit grower have been injured to that extent. The fruit grower is an honest man, but perhaps one in a hundred would be crooked in the packing of his fruit, and he has to be watched. There should be a proper system of inspection, and the inspector should exercise a little common sense in the carrying out of his duties; he should, you might IMr. Motherwell.]
say, temper justice with mercy. If he finds a man wrongfully packing, a man who, perhaps, did not understand the law, the inspector should show him his error and point out the requirements of the regulations. When I asked the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) if he did not vote for reciprocity in 1911 he quoted the words of Tennyson:
Yet I doubt not through the ages one increasing purpose runs,
And the thoughts of men are widened with the process of the suns.
Yes, I doubt not that in commercial matters we must be broadened out with the process of the suns, and that is why I direct attention to some of these matters affecting my province. The hon. member for Digby and Annapolis may not agree with my suggestion regarding the chief inspector, as he is now in the hon. member's county. But the counties of Hants, Kings and Annapolis are the fruit growing counties. In Hants fruit growing is increasing, and Kings produces sixty per cent of the apples of Nova Scotia. So I say to the minister that these matters should be adjusted, and the expenditure should not be cut down with the effect of making both the consumer and the producer suffer. The apple producer in Nova Scotia is not afraid of inspection; what he wants is a fair inspection by men who will do their duty without being elated over the job they hold and without trying to put down industry. The minister brags about the fact that the fruit of Canada arrives in Great Britain in first-class shape. Quite true, but that is altogether due to the fact that the honest producer of fruit in this country wants his goods to be put on the market in the best possible condition. That is why I ask for the provision of apple facilities at Halifax by way of heating and cooling houses on the piers so that the present difficulties in respect to the handling of fruit through that port may be overcome. When the fruit arrives at Halifax it is in good order, chilled or frozen, but it often becomes overheated, before it is put on the boats. I am not advocating anything particularly for Halifax; I am asking for facilities for the fruit growers of Nova Scotia. As I have already said, do not put it up to the Dominion Atlantic Railway. They are bound to get the traffic there anyhow, whether the result is good, bad or indifferent. The Canadian National will not do it; the Canadian National to us in western Nova Scotia is not worth a snap of the fingers. I ask the minister to go to his colleague the Minister of Public Works and demand that this be done. The thing we most need in Nova Scotia is

I should not like this

The hon. member describes them as No. 1 Fancy. I know what a No. 1 apple used to be. It has now been susperseded by an Extra Fancy. I am familiar with a Fancy apple. But I have not the least idea what a No. 1 Fancy is. It rather smacks of the mixture of thought which sometimes emanates from the oriental's brain, and I think it is possible that in some sections of the valleys of the interior the orientals may have invaded the realm of tree fruits, and have shipped out an article which they have chosem to call a " No. 1 Fancy." But whether it was fair or unfair on the part of the hon. memlber to bring these things here with the object of tainting the name of Okanagan fruit, I do not regret that he did so, because no finer argument could be advanced in favour of this inspection service which the growers in the interior of British Columbia have asked the Dominion government to help them to provide. It was a voluntary act on the part of the shippers of fruit. Their desire in asking for such an inspection was to demonstrate by their grade, by the accuracy with which their grade was maintained, that the exhibition fruit, which in international and imperial shows has demonstrated the unexcelled qualities of the Okanagan product, is of the same standard as their commercial pack. The fruit is grown in valleys of the interior that are pretty widespread and1 is collected in those valleys by various shipping houses. Many of them come under the control of the co-operative movement known as the Associated Growers of British Columbia. That associated head office has under its control from twenty to thirty "locals" and it is by the "locals" that the collecting and the shipping of apples is done. In addition there are a considerable number of independent fruit shippers, but they ship small amounts of fruit in comparison to the large quantity shipped by the Associated Growers. And so long as human nature is what it is, there will be times when the grading is not carried out in the best possible way, and if fruit inperfectly graded ever goes on the market in that way it is certain to bring trouble. That is the very reason why the growers voluntarily approached the

Dominion, government, through its fruit commissioner, to help them to put on such an inspection service that they would be helped in demonstrating to the wholesale trade that they were endeavouring at any rate, to live up to the grade that is stamped on their boxes. In reply to the hon.

Let me say that the Creston district in my constituency is a very promising one, and in the matter of carrying off prizes has been quite equal to the Okanagan district. The grower in the Creston district is doing everything possible to put the best grade of apples upon the prairie market; and I state before this committee that they consider the prairie market as one of their best markets. It has been stated too that the best grades go to the foreign market and that the inferior grade is used for home consumption. I believe I am quite safe in saying that that d'oes not work out. The apple growers endeavour to supply the best grade of apples for home consumption. Two or three of my prairie friends are eager to buy if they can be supplied with the best grade of apples; and the grower has agreed to supply that market with the ver3' best grade of apples that he can produce. In regard to the inspection, I again say that I am in close touch with the inspection of fruit throughout the Creston district, and this is the first time I have ever heard it stated by anyone that the matter of thorough inspection had been overlooked in any way. I have had some complaints from the growers; but as a whole the regulations have been working out fairly well, and

It depends on the variety.

Yes. These apples that
have been shown here probably went bad about two months ago, but there are apples that will be worthless in November and others in December. A Delicious No. 1 can be kept in cold storage and be of real value at this
time of year, but that does not necessarily apply to this apple. I am proud to know that there are in the House members from British Columbia who are capable of defending their own province; and I refer especially to the new member who represents the constituency of Yale (Mr. Stirling). That hon. gentleman certainly knows how to defend himself and his country and I am glad to have the opportunity of saying this word on his behalf. We should all be pleased to see the apple industry of this country develop and we should give it every encouragement. If the apple industry of British Columbia went down we should all be forced to buy our apples elsewhere. Of course, we should no doubt get supplies from Nova Scotia, but that province, being on the seaboard, commands an overseas market in England, and for that reason we do not use many of the Nova Scotian apples. A few years ago we got considerable quantities of the eastern fruit in Toronto and Montreal but there is a bigger demand for it in the Old Country. I must congratulate the province of Nova Scotia as well on its apple industry; undoubtedly there has been a great improvement in every respect. I remember the time when one could not get an honest apple from Nova Scotia any more than from Ontario, but to-day there is not. a province that ships out apples that are not fit for consumption. You can sit in your office and ship a consignment of apples from any one of 90 per cent of our packers, and without looking at the fruit rest assured that it will be free from criticism. That is what the act has done for us and the Department of Agriculture is to be complimented on its work. I am not referring particularly to the present department, but ever since the act came into force every minister over the department has approved of it. And why should they not? We are spending a lot of money in this connection and some day I hope we shall see perfection.

I am quite surprised that neither the minister nor his deputy has referred the committee to the section in the act which would easily answer all complaints made in regard to the selling of fruit. This summer a large quantity of peaches was shipped throughout the country and one dealer in Kingston had the misfortune to receive a large number of packages which were unfit for consumption.
Surely not.

If the hon. gentleman who makes that remark knows so much about fruit he ought to be aware of the pro-
Supply-Agriculture

vision in the act which would save him and others a few dollars in transactions of this kind. But whether or not the Department of Agriculture thinks fit to draw the attention of the public to this matter, I, for one, would feel that I had been remiss in my duty if I did not refer the committee to the section of the act which I have mentioned. If those who have made complaints had been aware of this provision it would have prevented the loss which they have incurred. This summer a large quantity of peaches was shipped from the Niagara district and sold, and a few days afterwards it was found that the fruit was unfit for consumption. I took the matter up with the department and I will give them credit for having referred me to the section of the act governing this matter. By that one action of the department the consumer in the city of Kingston was saved quite a few pennies. The section in question reads:
(7) No person shall sell, or offer for sale, any fruit in any package that is so diseased, wormy or otherwise depreciated as to render it unfit for consumption.
That provision appears on page 8 and it is sufficient to protect the consumer. If the fruit is not fit for consumption all he need do is return it. The dealer in Kingston refused to pay for the consignment of peaches and I was pleased to know that this section was in the act.. The consumer in all cases can have recourse to it, for it is intended for his protection. As I said a moment ago, I am surprised that the minister or his deputy did not mention the clause in reply to the complaints made.

Is there not also a
clause in the act providing for prosecution and summary conviction in case of misrepresentation.
Absolutely; it is all in the act.

Item agreed to.
Seed, feed and fertilizer control, $295,000.

The man who makes up the agricultural estimates deserves the description which one of our writers applied to King Charles I. He said that the king just before his death had confessed his sins in half an hour, ana' observed that he was a great master of condensation. The other estimates are all much more detailed than those of the Department of Agriculture; why, I do not know. In the agricultural estimates five or six million dollars is crushed into about eight or nine items: for example, there are live stock, $1,280,000; experimental farms $1,440,000; health of animals, $1,905,000, and so on. It seems to me that we could study

them in advance and compare them with other years much more easily if they were subdivided as is the case in Railways and Canals or in Public Works. I do not say that the minister initiated this plan; I do not know who did; it may have been the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), but the condensation is carried to an extreme. It means nothing at all to ibe told, "Live stock, $1,280,000 ", if the various activities of the Live Stock branch do not appear. If they were given half a dozen in number the estimates would be much more illuminating and one could study them in advance.

That criticism is well taken. I have not found it easy introducing reforms in this House; I have tried a few but I find that one runs up against a stone wall before he has got very far. To a large extent, therefore, I have been accepting these matters as I found them. If, however, my hon. friend will look more closely he will find! that the arrangement is different. I have here these votes subdivided however, into six or seven items. We have for example, for administration $11,000; subventions in connection with seed fairs, $77,500; Inspection and Sale Act-that is to say, the new Hay Act we have taken over this season for the first time-$12,000. Then we have laboratory and inspection services, which is a system of laboratories that extends across the country almost from ocean to ocean. The first of these is situated at Calgary and proviri'es for the inspection of grass and clover seeds, germinating tests, freedom from weed tests, and so on. That inspection applies to the whole five subdivisions into which Canada is divided. The next is at Winnipeg, and gives similar services. The next is at Toronto, the centre of the grass ana! clover seed business of the Dominion. The next is the central station here at Ottawa. There are also fees for chemical analyses; these are given to certain analysts who have authority to analyse the various brands of fertilizer placed on the market. Roughly speaking, that is the subdivision of the work under this branch, but it includes other services of minor importance.

Item No. 50: Seed,
feed and fertilizer control, $295,000.

Will the minister explain this vote?

Supply-Agriculture

We had five minutes on this vote before six o'clock. The leader of the opposition suggested that these votes be subdivided as to the various branches of expenditure, and I have concurred in that suggestion. I will give the subdivisions of each vote as we come to it.

Will the minister repeat
the subdivisions of this item, which he gave before six o'clock?

Administration costs, $11,000; subventions for seed fairs, $77,500, including production and markets; Inspection and Sales Act, $12,000; laboratory and inspection service, $180,000; fees for chemical analyses, $5,000; sundries, $10,000.

What progress is being
made in that branch which has to do with the improvement of seed?

About twenty years ago the Canadian Seed Growers' Association was organized with the idea of producing pure seed which would be true to variety. They have members all over Canada and they conduct a very active campaign in this direction. In Alberta a plant has been established for the cleaning of any of this registered seed that is offered for that purpose in order that it may be fitted for the market. It is impossible to put seed in first class condition for the market with the ordinary farm appliances, and by means of this seed cleaning apparatus they make the seed comply with the provisions of the Seed Control Act. There is a similar organization in Saskatchewan, with Moosejaw as its headquarters. During the last twenty years not only this registered seed but the various commercial seeds that are put on the market- clover, grass and garden seeds-have been greatly improved, and an export market has been established on account of the high quality of our product. Moreover, when seeds are imported our inspectors have samples sent to their laboratories and these are carefully inspected before they are allowed to go on the market. This service has also been extended to field and garden seeds such as beets, mangels, and the like. The Seed Control Act, which came into force a little over twenty years ago and has been twice revised, is admitted to be one of the best seed control acts on the continent.
Is this seed cleaning done in a central plant, or are there various plants throughout the Dominion?

In Alberta it is
done at one plant, and there is one in Quebec. It is purely a voluntary matter.

Are these not provincial
activities?

Oh, yes; they are
usually organized provincially, and in each case I think a good deal of assistance is given by the provincial government.

I know that Alberta has
recently established a seed cleaning plant but I was not aware that the Dominion had given any assistance to it.
Yes, we give them a grant.

What is the amount of the
grant ?

It dees not go to
the cleaning plants; these have only recently been established. The grant is for educational work generally and for the organization of seed fairs. The straight grant to the Seed Growers' Association is $10,000, and the amount under the head of production and markets, including subventions for seed fairs, is $77,500. This plan was adopted some fifteen years ago for the purpose of unifying seed fairs.
The Dominion held seed fairs, and the provinces also held seed fairs. Finally it was decided by the Dominion Seed branch that instead of holding Dominion seed fairs they would hand over the amount available for the purpose to be administered by the provinces, and that practice has been in vogue ever since. It was one of the steps taken to avoid overlapping. While it did not save us any money, it resulted in a consolidation of the work and, I think, yielded better results.

Is the ministei able to
tell us whether any money is still given to farmers who are trying to raise seed for seed purposes? I Temember that some years ago the federal authority used to give a subsidy, or an amount of some kind, to help the farmers to produce seed. In fact I remember that in the province of Quebec clover seed was grown by encouraging farmers to form co-operative associations and obtain the necessary machinery for the purpose. The province used to make a contribution, and I think the federal government also granted a certain amount towards the production of this seed. Since that time the province of Quebec has been growing its own clover seed, instead of making importations as it used to do. I think if we could aid the farmers to some extent in the way I have indicated it would have very good results.

My hon. friend the member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset) who is sitting beside me suggests $50. That might be a proper amount for wealthy men but in the case of poorer members they are satisfied with $5. When they go to a dealer they get what is called " No. 1 " seed but sometimes that seed is not what it professes to be. I would urge the minister and his officials to consider the matter and see whether aid of some kind cannot be granted. ' Mr. MOTHERWELL: I shall be very glad to consider my hon. friend's suggestion.

It is primarily on
the basis of population as nearly as it can be arrived at. Of course some provinces, by reason of their more efficient organizations, take greater advantage of the system. In other provinces there have not been organized so many seed fairs. At any rate the basis of apportionment is the population. But the farmers must organize locally before they are eligible for the grant.

Does the administration of
the Feeding Stuffs Act come under this vote?
Yes.

Last year that act was
amended. I should like the minister to State how it is working out in its amended form?

We have not had
a single complaint since. We were acting right on the straight in connection with that matter, although I noticed at the time there was a good' deal of suspicion as to what the object of the amendments was. However, I do not think we have had a single complaint since. Our miller friends are behaving beautifully.

Item agreed to.
For experiments in dehydration, $15,000.

This class of expenditure was first incurred two years ago for the first time for the purpose of utilizing some of our second' grade fruits. They were not exactly culls, but at the peak of the season it was felt that every -practicable means should be used -to take care of the peak crop when the fruit was ripening in order to save as much of it as possible from any ultimate damage. In view of the fact that millions of pounds of dried fruit of various kinds were coming into the country from the outside, it was felt that it would be a calamity to allow a lot of our own fruit to go to waste for the lack of some system of dehydration. Dehydrating is nothing but drying in accordance with the most scientific methods. There are members of the committee who can recall that apples used to be dried by hanging them round the kitchen stove pipe, a convenient roost for the flies. Later on the evaporated apple system came into vogue and it was a great improvement. Well, the dehydration system is just as -much an improvement on the evaporated method, as evaporation was an improvement on the old kitchen drying system, and three experimental plants have been put up, one at Grimsby to take care of the Niagara peninsula, one at Ottawa, and the other one at Penticton in the


Supply-Agriculture
Okanagan valley. I do not know that I can furnish any evidence yet that capitalists are prepared to put the necessary money into a plant; but we are demonstrating the feasibility, and the practicability of it, and the quality of the goods. They are being recognized as very much superior to dried fruit and almost equal to green fruit. That is the position, and that is what this vote is for.
Have the experiments upto-date been profitable? Have you demonstrated the profitableness of the venture?

As we are experimenting with such comparatively small quantities, we have to make an estimate as to that; but we figure that it will be profitable. Really a commercial plant would be much larger than these plants I refer to, and making allowance for that fact we think it will be profitable. There is no reason why it should not be.

Can the
minister tell us how dehydrated fruit is received by the public? I have noticed that it is offered for sale in certain stores in this city, and perhaps the minister has some figures as to how the public are receiving it.

We have had
samples of it in the offices here, and a good many hon. members took pleasure in sampling it, because it tasted " real good," and the public have taken to it well. It is -a matter of keeping it before the public. That is a practical way of advertising it and I think will get the result.

What is the difference in
the effect between dehydration and evaporation on the tissue of the fruit itself?

I think the secret
of it is that the dehydration is done under better conditions and the fruit is not subject to the constant change of air, and the effect on the tissue is not the same. Dehydration is very -much more favourable because of the fact that the product retains the flavour of the green fruit better than in the case of any other method.
Dehydration does not break down the cells the same as evaporation does?
I think not.

What is the difference in
the cost of dehydration as compared with evaporation?
We have no figures on that. It is pretty hard to get figures sufficiently reliable; and furthermore we have not an evaporation plant.
I understand the handling is about the same, but what is the difference in the consumption of fuel?
We have only one plant. In order to make an intelligent comparison we would require to have an evaporating plant running at the same place.

I understand it (requires only half as much fuel in the one case as the other. What was the nature of the test they had in British Columbia? What quality' of fruit d'o you use for best quality of dehydrated product?

It is just like anything else, the better the fruit you use the better the dehydrated product would be; but we can use a second grade fruit, which otherwise would be a drug on the market; and in this way we prevent that waste. First class fruit would make a good dehydrated product but there is no particular object in putting first class fruit into dehydrated plants, because it could be sola' on the market. In the same way you would not want to make pulp-wood out of first class timber although I believe it is sometimes done.
How many pounds of fresh apples are required for one pound of evaporated fruit and how many pounds would be required for the dehydrated fruit?

We have not that information. To make a real test between this system and the evaporating system all along the line, we would require to have both systems. The principal object we had in mind was to take care of a lot of second grade fruit as the season was approaching when it would be a glut on the market. We desired to put it on the market in a more toothsome and acceptable condition than ordinary dried fruit. There is really a prejudice against dried fruit, if it is not well done. However, there is not sufficient prejudice to prevent enormous quantities of it coming into Canada. Apparently they have it down to a greater science in other countries than we have reached in Canada; otherwise I cannot imagine why so much is imported. Plums, apricots and apples come into Canada in enormous quantities, running into the millions, and our aim is to put a better article on the market by means of this dehydration.

Our information

I understand, that dehydrated fruit is taking the place of dried fruit in California to such an extent that, whereas in 1922 there were only four plants in California, last year there were 1,500. This is the third or fourth time that I recall this vote having come up in the estimates, and I am wondering how long this experiment will have to be conducted to get conclusive results. Perhaps the minister can give us some information as to what further results may be expected if the experiments are carried on this year.

This is only the
second year that I can recall-and my deputy confirms me in my statement-that we have had this vote.
The estimate of last year was $10,500, I think.

Yes, then this is
the second year.

I mean for
the year before.
Mr.' MOTHERWELL: Let us put it then at three years. This is more or less like any other class of investigation work. We do not expect to sow to-day and reap to-morrow in this world. It is a sort of missionary work. You have to cast your bread upon the waters and sometimes wait for many days to get returns. At this time when there is not much capital seeking investment, you cannot expect many results. There are many reasons why there is not much capital seeking investment. In the first place, capital would want to see this a little further demonstrated. Moreover, we have labour and other troubles that make capital timid at this particular time, and I would be surprised to see a great deal of capital invested in this right now. Later on, -when capital is not so timid, is freer, I hope to see investments, if we can demonstrate in the meantime that this is good business. Judging from the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) and from our own information that large quantities of dehydrated fruit have been coming in from the United States, I see no reason why we should not be able to dehydrate just as well in Canada. So far, we have not done so. We have been keeping on importing the foreign goods. We have no estimate how long we shall have to continue this experiment, but I would imagine that we shall have to continue it for two or three years more.

I was desirous of finding out whether there was any hope of achieving any result, or whether the de-

Supply-Agriculture
partment is simply tiding this over for a further period. What is the nature of this vote? Is it for experimental purposes, or is it simply to keep this product on the market?

For both purposes. It is to demonstrate that dehydration can be done in Canada and also to take care of the surplus fruit. Some varieties are better adapted for putting on the market in a green state. Others, that are less acceptable for putting on the market in a green state, can be put on the market in a dehydrated state. One would not think of putting on the market as pulpwood some of our finest timber. It is timber, of inferior quality that is put on the market as pulpwood.

The minister does not get my point. We do not maintain an experimental bureau year after year in order to demonstrate to the lumbermen of this country that they should not put certain timber on the market as pulpwood. It has been pretty well demonstrated, through these experiments and experiments in the United States, that dehydration is a success and can be just as successful in Canada as elsewhere. If that is so and there is nothing further to be gained in the way of experiments, why continue this vote from year to year?

Would my hon.
friend suggest a period at which he thinks this experiment should terminate? The committee will remember that the other day we ceased demonstration work in connection with the dairy business, the Finch creamery. That was run for twelve or thirteen years as a demonstration to show that a large creamery was capable of turning out butter and cheese and of handling milk and cream. It took twelve years to get the full advantage of that experiment. After having sold it to a private company, we were still adversely criticised because we did not keep it on. We concluded that we had come to the end of that experiment; that we had made the demonstration, and yet we were criticised for parting with it. My hon. friend wants to know why we do not discontinue this experiment at [DOT] the end of two or three years. I do not think twelve years will be necessary to demonstrate this properly; but in addition to experiments as to the acceptability of fruit when it is dehydrated, there are other experiments as to what particular varieties of fruit lend themselves best to dehydration and what it is best to put on the markets in a green state. That will take some years to demonstrate, and I
do not think my hon. friend should be in too great haste to terminate this experiment. It is doing good work and we will not run it one year longer than necessary.

Are experiments being
carried on in regard to other fruits than apples?
Yes, all fruits.

I do not
wish the minister to misconstrue my attitude in this matter. Although I come from a province which does not engage in the production of fruit, I would not want it to be supposed that I am opposed to experiments along this line. I have, however, observed that it is sometimes difficult to discontinue these experiments and inquiries that we start in this House, and it is well that we keep our eye on these points. If the minister can show us-and that is the question which I have asked him-that there is actual reason why this experiment should be carried on with the hope of good results, I am in favour of carrying it on to the extent of twelve years, if necessary, but I want to be sure that it is being carried on with some prospect of definite results.

I think I have
shown my hon. friend, in the case of the Finch creamery, that we can stop these experiments, return to the government treasury the full amount that was expended and also distribute a very large amount of money amongst the farmers of the district. We do not hope to have such magnificent financial results in this case, but we hope to d'emon-strate to capital that this is a good business in which to invest money. This is not a particularly attractive time for capital, and we should not stop in the middle of an experiment of this character, but should proceed.

Good live stock being one of the determining factors in the improvement of agriculture, I may be pardoned for saying a word or two in regard to this industry. I wonder if the minister or the government have entirely given up the notion of effecting better trade relations with the United States? The rearing of live stock can only be profitable if we secure proper markets for its disposal. Our logical market is to the south. I do not wish to minimize the importance of the home market, which I think is the best, but the next in importance for live stock, as well as for other farm products, is certainly that to the south. In 1923 we shipped 120,947 head of cattle to the United States, in 1924,
183,000,	and in former years our shipments were even larger, amounting in 1920 to as high as 500,000 head. In spite of the fact that we are penalized by a duty of $20 per head entering that market, we have to send them there anyway.

The fact that the government of the United States have raised the tariff walls so high 25
that we can scarcely see over them does not lead to the conclusion that it is of no use to negotiate with them with a view to the securing of better trade relations. Many of them have taken prizes in very good classes at Chicago, Toronto and other large shows. They are, however, very much lacking in having a suitable sire for su-ch an important place. If the minister would use a part of this vote to assist in getting the right type of animal, he would be well ahead of the other breeders in the community and the farm would then render a real service. I believe the herd there is somewhat in the neighbourhood of a score of female animals and

the minister would do well to carry out this suggestion. I have another suggestion to make when we come to the next item, but I trust the minister will see that this suggestion is given consideration. I was not altogether satisfied
with the minister's reply to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) when the latter referred to the desirability of closer trade relations with the United States as respects cattle. About three weeks ago I was present at the annual convention of the Illinois Agricultural Association held at Champaign-Urbana where there were present about 800 delegates and 400 visitors. I was there for two days and I embraced the opportunity extended to me to interview as many of the delegates as possible, all of whom are representative farmers from that state, in an attempt to find out from them their attitude as regards the entry of Canadian cattle, that is feeder cattle, to the middle west. I did not meet a single delegate who was not in favour of reducing or abolishing the duty. You may say that these men were not frank with me in view of the fact that I had gone down there on their invitation as a Canadian visitor. But in my judgment they were frank with me, because the same delegates who told me that they were in favour of the abolition of the duty on cattle also informed me that they were in favour of an immediate increase in the duty on Canadian butter. If I mistake not, that convention appointed a delegation to go from there to Washington with a demand that the duty on Canadian butter entering the United States be immediately increased. I make this statement in the hope that the minister and the officials of his department are fully aware of the sentiment existing in the middle west at present with regard to the entry of our cattle into the United States. There is nothing at all unselfish in the attitude of those people towards us; they are demanding our cattle to-day because they believe they can make money on the finishing. If the agriculturists are in favour of allowing our cattle in free, surely the consumers in the United States cannot possibly be opposed to their entry. I think we might in this way obtain reciprocity piecemeal. There is a demand in western Canada, as the minister knows, for the entry of Wisconsin dairy cattle free, and I have often wondered whether he could not with

If there is one we never
heard of it.

With regard to the suggestion of the hon. member (Mr. Hoey) we had ambitions two or three years ago of trying to accomplish what he suggested, that is to say, to bring about a sort of reciprocity piecemeal; and in the estimates of two years ago we provided something like $6,000 of a grant to an organization with headquarters in Calgary, whose primary object was to promote trade relations with the United States in cattle. They had an emissary in the United States and were developing various markets andl we felt that we were going as close to securing a market of that kind in that roundabout way as we dared, having regard to ordinary international courtesies which demand that we do not interfere with another county's business. It was just about that time, or prior to that, that Mr. Manning Doherty met with a good deal of criticism in the United Kingdom for pursuing his activities contrary to the orthodox methods. I am not
entering into the pros and cons of that matter, but if he got results, most of us, I suppose, are not worrying as to how he obtained them. Any port in a storm is an old saying that sometimes is very appropriate. But there are international courtesies that must be observed; and to take part in any indirect method of trying to get into a market by a side door rather than through the front door is very apt to lead to difficulties. Take, for instance, the preference which was promised on fruit by the British government and which was afterwards retracted. There was a very strong effort made by some of the fruit growers in Canada at that time to have us intervene with the British government and try to induce them to stand by their original pllian of a preference for our fruit. Now, that is a very delicate matter and I would point out to my hon. friend that a similar delicacy characterizes this cattle business. As a matter of fact we went as far as we felt we could go and get away with it.

Public opinion may have
changed since then.

Possibly; and I
think that it is changing. They will not pursue their present course indefinitely because it seems to me to be a false attitude. It is only a matter of time, when foodstuffs go up sufficiently high and the people in the United States cry for cheaper articles, when there will be access given to our stock. But whether we can get our cattle in by means of these local activities to which I have referred is doubtful, although I tried' it, with the dangers I have mentioned apparent on all sides.

One of the drawbacks in the transportation of cattle from western Canada is the fact that the animals lose condition on the long rail route from Winnipeg to the Atlantic coast. That difficulty could be overcome if the Hudson Bay railway were completed. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) last year made a trip through the Hudson bay country, although he did not go the whole way, and in an interview published in the Manitoba Free Press in September he was quoted as having said that as soon as he got back to Ottawa and met with his colleagues he would do his very best to see that the railway was finished right up to Port Nelson. Cattle, as we well know, do not lose condition on the ocean trip, but they certainly do on a long rail route, and the thousand miles between Winnipeg and Montreal might be eliminated through the use of Port Nelson. And Port Nelson is just as
