near to Liverpool as is Montreal. This, however, is by the way. What I want particularly to refer to is the matter of horse clubs for which $25,000 is being asked. I do not want the minister to run away with the idea that I am opposed' to these clubs, for I do not object to federal assistance to horse breeders. I do think, however, that there is need for a little change in the operation of these institutions. Some of the parties feel that they have a grievance in the working of the rules, and this grievance could be obviated if section 6 of the act providing federal assistance, page 13, were eliminated1. That section provides that the owner or owners of a stallion shall not belong to a club. I should like to see that provision repealed. Horses are becoming scarce in every part of Canada; indeed, they are becoming scarce throughout the world. There is a scarcity of horses in the eastern provinces, according to the official figures, and in western Canada there will not be many available for shipment. Stallions of high quality certainly are scarce. To get the benefit of federal assistance it is necessary that horse breed'ers should hire a stallion and at present there are very few that can be hired; they must be purchased outside and brought in. But private individuals cannot afford the risk of purchasing high priced sires. Consequently the businesslike way is for a number of fanners to form a company, put up the necessary cash and select one or two of their number to purchase a good stallion; but simply because they are working in that businesslike manner they are penalized; they get no federal assistance. The Breeders' Gazette of the United States in its issue of January 15 last has the following editorial:
The majority of the work animals are nine years old or over; many of them being twelve to fifteen years of age. Many farmers are already looking about for pairs of horses or more for next season's work, and finding it difficult to locate the really good type of horse that they have been accustomed to use. The net result of all this is that there is a general feeling among farmers in the combelt states east of the Missouri that breeding must be re-established.
The editor continues:
The most practical method is for ten or twelve men in the community to organize a corporation capitalized at a few thousand dollars in shares of $100 each. The expense of incorporating with the assistance of a friendly lawyer or banker will usually not amount to more than $50. As many shares can be sold as may seem necessary for the purchase of a horse, and the balance of the stock held in the treasury. Fifteen shares sold to fifteen separate farmers will raise $1,500 in cash; and two men of unquestioned integrity, who are good judges of horses, can take the money and go direct to the stable of any dealer or breeder and buy a very good horse, ship him home, and still have a little money left over.

We have associations in this country doing identical work, but they can get no federal assistance for the simple reason that the clause of the act which I have quoted excludes the stallion owner or owners, as the case may be, from belonging to a club. We know that horses are going to be scarce in a year or two, and if we wait until there is an absolute shortage before we begin breeding operations we will find ourselves in trouble.
To-day I endeavoured to obtain from the Live Stock branch figures of the number of horses in Canada, but without success. However, I have the figures given at Toronto on February 12, by the president of the Clydesdale Horse Association. He said:
"While the total shows an increase as compared with 1923, the number of colts and fillies shows a decrease. As compared with 1919 the number of colts and fillies or young stock coming on to supply the annual wastage shows a decrease of 291,100. There is a decrease of over 13,000 in the number of colts and fillies in 1924 as compared with 1923. The number of stallions in Canada shows a decrease of 20.492 since 1919, or nearly 42 per cent. The figures show a decrease of 10,554 the largest decrease in any one year since 1919.
Horses show an increase last year in every province excepting Ontario and New Brunswick as compared with 1923, the decrease in Ontario being around 10,000. The greatest decrease in the number of stallions is in the western provinces, 1,694 in Manitoba, 5,278 in Saskatchewan, and 2,625 in Alberta.
There is a decrease of 18,000,000 horses, mules and asses taking world conditions all over. The question is, what is to be done to encourage farmers to go into the breeding of horses. It is well known that there are many indifferent sires travelling at a very low fee, consequently the high priced stallions have to compete with them unless they are clubbed, and the really good sires are not being used. It must also be borne in mind that the farmers who have been sufficiently well off to purchase high class sires are in many cases quitting the business, and the young men taking their places do not care to invest money in horse breeding. In my district there has been what you may call a horse club, a horse association, or a horse syndicate, going steadily for 25 years, and yet we are finding it very difficult to carry on, simply because we can get no federal assistance. We are doing our utmost to purchase the best sires available. In proof of what I say, allow me to read a cablegram which I received on January 23:
Can ship genuine good horse rising five years able win international well bred, price five hundred pounds. Cable reply.
James Kilpatrick, Kilmarnock.
I had to turn down that offer because our people felt that they could not afford to put up the money without federal assistance. Last

year we had on the road the grand champion of Brandon in 1919 and yet that stallion in competition with the poorest grade of horses only had a season of 42 mares where he generally had 100. That is going to put our association absolutely out of business, for on account of scarcity we find it next to impossible to hire or club a horse. Besides, there are disadvantages. In hiring a stallion for a season you may not get the same horse the second year, and it is well understood that a sire has got to travel in the district four or five seasons to get the best results. I should like the minister to consider this proposition, for at present those who are doing their level best to purchase good sires co-operatively are being discriminated against as though they were criminals.

Touching the. last
point first, I think the remedy for meeting the competition made by the cheaper stallion would be to raise the standard of the pure bred stallions. I understand that Manitoba has a law prohibiting the travelling of any but pure bred animals. Is not that right?
Yes, but that does not prevent them standing at home.

That is right, you
can hardly prohibit a man keeping any kind of stallion he wants to for his own use at home. I know in the province of Saskatchewan we introduced the principle of a licensed stallion area, with a board to examine the animals that were allowed to travel in those municipalities, and this raised the quality of the stallions immediately. In Manitoba the principle was adopted generally all over the province at the outset, and I think there must be a marked improvement there. You will have to develop a desire on the part of breeders to use the best animals available. With regard to the other objection raised by my hon. friend, that no stallion owner shall belong to a club, the primary object of this regulation is that the club is intended to help, not the stallion owner, but rather the man who has no stallion. If you permitted stallion owners to become members of a
10 p.m. horse club, they would be getting the benefit of the use of their own horses and the government's subsidy as well. I am sure my hon. friend must recollect that years ago in the west before the horse club business was organized the owners of stallions used to go all over the country organizing syndicated stallions, and with their natural desire for gain, and with no supervision of the animals, a bunch of farmers would be
hoaxed, with the result that when these clubs came in the desire was to help not so much the stallion owner as the man without a stallion in an effort to improve the horse breeding industry. There may be a hardship on some, but speaking generally I think it is a wise provision.

What is the difference between twenty farmers hiring a stallion and twenty farmers purchasing a stallion? Why should they be benefactors of the country in the one case and criminals in the other? If the stallions are not to be had here and they go overseas and purchase, why should they be discriminated against? That is the point I wish to make, and the point that the minister has not seen yet.
We will give that somewhat delicate matter further consideration.
Is the minister lessening his activities under this vote?

Where we can
make arrangements with the province to take over some of the activities that are essentially associated with production, yes. In the provinces that are not ready for that, we will continue.

The activities in the matter of cow testing represented an expenditure last year of something over $40,000, and this year they have been taken from the Dairy branch and put under the Live Stock branch; yet the vote is the same this year as last. Two carloads of eggs coming from the United States were turned back at the border because they were unfit for human consumption, so that this inspection is very necessary.

I think it did exist for a year or two.

I quite understand that, yet the incumbent of the portfolio of agriculture must have something to say in determining the financial policy of the government.
Do I understand the minister to say that you can use a stale egg for cooking purposes? Is it possible to use in pastry eggs that are unfit for food when used in any other manner?

I am sure my hon. friend has often heard the expression, "Well, it is not just up to the mark but it is all right for cooking purposes." I would not like to say just where the line is. There is a certain

staleness that makes an egg objectionable for eating either boiled or fried, but which still permits it to be used in pastry or for cooking
purposes.
The minister cannot explain how it is that a stale egg may be all right for cooking when it cannot be used for anything else.
I suppose it is spiced up with all sorts of niceties to disguise it- that may be the reason.
The addition of the spices would hide the real flavour of the egg?
The egg would be, there to do the lightening and the spice to give it taste.

A disease known as European fowl plague has struck the poultry of ten or twelve of the states, and the United States government have themselves quarantined all these states. We have put an embargo against the states that they themselves have quarantined, and that embargo is still on.

There is a feature of
the live stock question, particularly as regards poultry, that I should like to draw to the attention of the minister, "and that is the importation of baby chicks from the United States due, I believe, to a recent ruling of the Post Office Department by which these birds can come in by parcel post. The columns of every Canadian agricultural paper were flooded during the past season with advertisements from large American poultry hatcheries, with the result that hundreds of thousands of baby chicks were brought into Canada. I believe these birds have been brought in to the detriment of the Canadian poultry industry. At the experimental farm we have a record of performance in order to raise the standard of the production of the Canadian hen. I believe that work is carried on at great expense and for a worthy purpose. The Ontario government is doing work along similar lines, and I believe they have accomplished very beneficial results in raising the standard of production. Under the circumstances why should all this work, or a great deal 6f it, be lost by the introduction of inferior chicks from the United States? In view of the price at which these birds are offered I believe they have no records of production behind them-they are simply ordinary chicks. I do not think we can afford to go on spending money year after year building up the standard of our Canadian live stock and then, with respect to one particular branch of it, nullify the whole work in one single season. I think there must be something done to find a remedy, either by a working arrangement with the Post Office Department or by some other method.

The embargo that
I spoke of with respect to disease will keep them out from all but a dozen of the American states, for the present year anyhow, but I have a question to ask my hon. friend. I am sure there is a lot to be said in behalf of this contention, but I should like to hear him show cause why the man who wants to buy these chicks should be deprived of the opportunity of doing it. Before there is a sale by the United States poultry man there must be a purchaser in this country. He sends an order to the American poultryman that he wants a hundred day-old chicks. Now it is impossible to tell how these chickens are bred; you do not even know what breed they belong to or even what age a great many of

them are. You do not know how they are registered or anything about them except that they are chicks. They may be two or three days old but they are usually called "baby chicks". How could I defend the keeping of them out when there are a lot of people in this country who want to buy them? I am honestly looking for information because I think I should like to see what my hon. friend suggests carried out. Is my hon. friend not afraid there is something like a protective suggestion about his proposition. I am not joking now, I should like to know how to get over the difficulty.

I am not scared because the minister has introduced the word "protection" in the expectation probably that I would throw up my hands. I think if the minister will look through the record of the Ontario Department of Agriculture he will find all kinds of regulations for saving the farmer from himself. All kinds of criticism has been indulged in with respect to pamphlets that have been scattered abroad to attract immigrants to Canaa'a. I am almost a convert to my hon. friend's contention, for the simple reason that there is no way of checking that up. Under the Customs Act pure bred animals, or animals used for breeding purposes are let in free. Under that section chicks that profess to be pine bred, although nobody can tell whether they are pure bred or not, are let in free. They are often scrub stuff and do our poultry business no good; and because of the impossibility of checking a chick and ascertaining whether it is what 
it pretends to be, I believe some minimum valuation should be put upon a chick before it is permitted to come in. Possibly we may take action before the session is over. Would you apply the
Dumping Act there?

The government of that day put a valuation of $50 a head on these bronchos, and compelled them to pay duty on that amount, and that had the effect of keeping out many cheap horses. Yes, I recall that
incident.

delightful and entertaining. Here we have my hon. friend from the great free trade party in Canada a Simon-pure free trader-

same time I think I can draw a distinction between protection, as advocated by my hon. friends to the right, and the protection that the hon. member for East Peterborough is wanting in this regard.

I am not altogether endorsing all that he said; I want to point out simply the difference between the protection advocated by my hon. friends to the right and the protection that the hon. member for East Peterborough is speaking about. I know my hon. friends are sometimes very anxious to put words into our mouths and to place us in a false position. letter he stated that he bad entirely lost confidence in the Conservative party in Canada and he hoped that some other friends from the other side of the House would join with some of the Progressive members and form a truly national party that would' do something to save this country from the position in which it was.

I have heard that in
Montreal too and1 I have passed my blessing on it. May it take place. I have never stood between my friends to the left and the gentlemen across the floor. Let them get together in the same camp and quit the camouflage, the sham. Let them walk on together and then we shall have a showdown in this Dominion and see what the people of this country want.

The right hon member used that very same expression "camouflage" last year. I do not know anything about camouflaging. I said not "members on the other side," but "some particular members on the other side" that are not very popular in their own quarters.
Who are they?
Oh, oh.

That is a principle you
must not talk about.

I hope hon. members are
getting a little pleasure out of this. I have got it and I hope we have all got it. There is in this House to-night a spirit of good feeling and fellowship that I have not seen for a long time, and we are indebted to the hon. member for East Peterborough for bringing about that state of affairs.
My hon. friend says that he is prepared to stand on his principles. A moment ago he said that his principle was free trade, but he is not going to practise it. Where is he standing?
What has this to do with sick cattle?
It is sick chickens, I think, we are talking about. How is my hon. friend going to protect the Canadian pure bred hen?

I did not say that I would
protect it.
He says that he is going to do this by the process the minister is following that is, by valuating them at forty cents apiece, although he knows quite well-

I admit that my hon.
friend is very chary about the word "protection". It is, however so difficult to distinguish between his meaning and his words that I find my vocabulary too limited altogether. How is he going to do it? He is going to do it by valuating these chicks at forty cents apiece, which is admitted by the minister- and the minister will not charge me with misstating the facts-is almost if not quite equal to an embargo.

No. High class
chickens are worth that.
It is intended to keep out the ordinary chicken, is it not?

Yes, a poor one,
but not a good one.

By putting on a valuation that certainly is not there. Supposing we were to apply that to our principle of protection, that we were to value all goods coming into this country at twice or three times their value to prevent them from coming in, what would our hon. friends say to us? We do not advocate any such extreme protection; but we say frankly that Canadian industry, whether it is the poultry industry, manufacturing industry, woollen industry, or agricultural industry in any of its branches, should be protected against unfair competition from the outside. For the leader of the party tc my left to repudiate all idea of protection and talk about principles of free trade, but the impracticability of it, is all nonsense and moonshine. It is about time that we faced in this House the main principles of division in the trade policy of this country. One is a drift towards a freedom of imports, a freedom from import duty on the part of imports, and the other is a sufficient protection to Canadian industry against competition from the outside.

If there is to be any
protective policy on baby chicks coming into this country, I want to protest, because frequently I have had occasion to ship in baby chicks and eggs for hatching purposes, and the man who is going to use these chicks should be considered as well. If we are going to protect the Canadian breeders, that is a different question.
There may be something to be said for the policy of protection that is at present being advocated by my hon. friends to the right. One thing that has amazed me for many years in connection with protection is that the real protectionist was always a free trader when the matter was one of farm production. I am glad to see that it is getting on a more logical
basis. As a farmer I maintain that if it can be shown to be beneficial, it is perfectly logical for the exponent of the policy of protection to ask for protection on farm products too, although in my opinion the farmer cannot be protected. That is what was done in the United States. The farmers there fought protection for a long time, but they realized that protection was going to be the policy of the country and they demanded a share of the benefits. If protection is going to be the policy of this country, then any benefits that might accrue from that policy should be shared by the fanners as well as others. Therefore, I say that my hon. friends in the new policy that they are advocating to-day are putting it on a more logical basis than it has ever been before.
Since the question of cattle marketing has been interjected into the debate under this item, has the minister had any reason during the last year to consider this question of marketing chilled and frozen beef in the old country?

No, we have not
conducted any more experiments than we reported last year.

I suggested something to the minister last year. I am not sure that I have any concrete proposals, but I should like to impress upon him the necessity of looking into this question a little further. From what study I have given of the subject, I am thoroughly convinced that if we can press it far enough we can eventually establish a very profitable market for chilled and frozen beef in the British Isles. We are discussing cattle rates and we are prepared to enter into an agreement with a company and bonus them to a large extent to carry our cattle overseas. I contend, as I have always done, that that is not a proper trade to build up at all. We were told a few years ago that the British people did not want chilled beef, but the figures disprove that. I have here the report for trade and navigation of the United Kingdom for the calendar year ending December 31, 1924, showing that there was imported into the Old Country for home consumption fresh meat to the extent of 34,969 hundredweights, a very small quantity, whereas in chilled beef we find that the British Isles imported 8,307,276 hundredweights from Uruguay and the Argentine republic as well as from some smaller countries. And classified as frozen meat we find importations amounting to 4,226,000 tons. The total importations of beef including a small amount of salted meat are given as 13,630,000 hundredweights. So that after all
Supply-Agriculture

the great volume of the beef consumption of the Old Country, at least of importations- because they have a fresh meat production at home-consists of chilled and frozen beef. A good many people claim that we cannot compete on an equal basis with the Argentine republic, and we have heard it frequently stated also that we are unable to compete with New Zealand in butter. I am not prepared to admit any of that; I contend that we can compete with any of these nations notwithstanding any question of distance or transportation difficulties or anything else. With the price of our land, the quality of the soil and the ability of our farmers to produce we can compete with the Argentine or any other country. But it needs energy and hard work to develop a market. Most of our beef shipped overseas is grain-fed, of a superior quality to the Argentine product. I think the deputy minister is on record as saying that a great deal of our chilled beef is thawed out and sold on the British market as British fresh beef. We get the price of chilled beef for it but it is sold at a large profit by the retailer.
I am not sure that I have any constructive suggestions to offer the minister, but this is something that the department should look into carefully. When we examine these figures and see the enormous quantities of this particular product consumed in the Old Country, and when we reflect that the consumption of this class of beef is increasing rapidly there, we should make some special effort to meet the situation. I am not very sure whether it will ever be practicable to ship live beef into the British market. There are a good many things that may help us; we are trying, for example, to secure a lower ocean rate, and another thing that might help us would be the securing of a reasonable grain rate from Winnipeg to Quebec over the Transcontinental. If we could ship mixed cargoes out of Quebec, including grain and cattle, we could handle the cattle through that port at from S4 to $5 per head cheaper than from Montreal. That is another question which I may discuss at some other time, and although I do not suggest that the minister should carry out any experiment at a loss such as he told us was incurred two years ago, I do think that he ought to examine into this question further and see whether something cannot be done to get us a share of this chilled and frozen beef trade.

I am sorry to disagree with
my hon. friend (Mr. Campbell), but I do not think he thoroughly understands what he is talking about; when he says that our chilled beef goes over to the Old Country and

is thawed out I am sure he does not. Our beef does not need to be thawed out for it is only chilled. When he talks about our competing with the Argentine republic I do not agree with him. The Argentine is a wonderful beef country and we can compete with them only from the standpoint of the shorter distance from Canada to the Old Country. It takes thirty days to bring meat from the Argentine to England and you cannot carry chilled meat that length of time. I contended in this House last year that our geographical position placed us in a favourable position to carry on a chilled meat trade, and I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce to make the experiment. Where we have fallen down in the past has been in our lack of a regular supply. When I was in the butcher business in the Old Country, if you came with beef from Canada my first question would have been whether I could get a supply of the same quality next week and the week after, and the week after that, so that I could tell my customer who enjoyed his Sunday dinner that I could supply him with the same sort of meat regularly. That is the important thing, and the minister knows that this is the condition with our butter. We have to have a regular supply. I agree that the live meat business is one in regard to which there is not much hope; a great deal of the proceeds is consumed in the rail and ocean rates. I am sure that if the minister would try the experiment I have suggested it would produce satisfactory results. But it must not be spasmodic; it must be carried on week by week for at least six months. The trouble in the past has been that beef going from here chilled was not supplied in a continuous volume; we shipped a quantity this week and shipped none for three weeks. An attempt of that kind certainly cannot succeed.

Perhaps I was wrong in referring to chilled beef having to be thawed out, but in other respects my hon. friend (Mr. Sales), after declaring that he did not agree with me, has endorsed practically every word I said. He pointed out that if we continued the trade long enough we could build it up permanently. Beef from the Argentine must Joe frozen, and although it may be classified as chilled beef it is in reality partly frozen when it reaches the United Kingdom. Our beef is in refrigeration for about seven days as against twenty-one days or more in the case of the Argentine product, and that puts the Canadian beef in a different class. I would, therefore, take what my hon. friend says as an endorsation of my

remarks, and I believe the minister would be well in his rights in carrying out this experiment. This problem is one that concerns not only the west but eastern Canada as well, and if we build up a profitable trade in chilled and frozen beef we do not need to worry about ocean rates; that question will solve itself.

Having lost so much money on the first shipment we did not feel that we had more money to throw away on the experiment, particularly when we knew that one of the packing companies sent about one hundred consecutive shipments extending over a year and lost money on all with the exception of two on which they broke even and two on which they made a profit. I simply wanted to check up the abattoirs to see whether our figures would correspond with theirs, and they tallied exactly. In the light of their continuous losses for over a year in about a hundred shipments, and our pronounced loss in the one shipment we made, I have not much hope of success even if we observe the conditions suggested by the hon. member, (Mr. Sales). Before you can get the best results you must have a continuous supply of acceptable meat from week to week, so that when the customers get used to it they will buy it regularly. But even with that advantage the abattoir people, with the four exceptions I have indicated out of one hundred, have lost money. In the light of that I did not feel justified in taking more chances of losing money at the present time. I would have no objection to trying it out again if the committee, particularly those members closely interested in the live stock industry, consider it to be worth while. But is it wise to do so when we are almost certain to lose out? I am very glad we conducted the experiment, because it gave us first hand information and removed the suspicion entertained by some that the abattoir experiment was not 'quite bona fide. To-day I believe it was.

Has the minister studied the
figures of the experiment carried on by the Harris Abattoir Company?
Yes.

I did not know that we would reach this item of chilled meat to-night. I have the figures submitted to me by Mr. McLean, of the Harris Abattoir Company, and it is apparent that the shipments were a long way from being regular, in fact they were most emphatically what might be termed spasmodic. Any experiment so carried* on is bound to fail. If the minister will look up 26
the figures I think he will find my assertion is correct.

Would the minister advise the committee whether it is not a fact that the people of the Argentine, our greatest competitors, own their ranches, their lines of steamships, and their retail shops all over Great Britain? I think that is perhaps the idea in the minds of hon. gentlemen here when they talk of the proposed experiment. I do not think the Harris Abattoir Company conducted their experiment in that way. I make the suggestion-I believe it has been made before-that if the minister established a couple of retail stores in the larger cities of Great Britain and guaranteed shipments regularly, a trade could be established in chilled meat. It seems to me it is a very opportune time, particularly when we have in prospect a line of steamships to carry over our stuff at reduced rates. I dissociate myself from the protectionist remarks voiced by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell). While he does not believe in protection for the farmer, yet he gives a mild endorsation to the principle.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) misunderstood me entirely; I did not advocate protection at alL

I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that if the farmer were given protection in any particular, it would be used as an excuse by the protected interests to ask for increased protection, so that in the long run the percentage of protection to the farmer would be nil; consequently we would be losers in the end. I would bring the protected interests down to our footing rather than attempt to reach their level, because they have the whip hand.

I understand that
officials of the Harris Abattoir Company expressed the opinion that if they had been able to carry on the experiment long enough with a regular flow of products to the retailers the trade in the end would have been quite profitable. I have that second hand, but I think I am quite safe in stating it as authentic.

Mr. Chairman, I have a
great deal of sympathy with what was said earlier in the discussion this afternoon about some of us being compelled to listen to explanations over and over again. Let me point out to the minister that we have passed several items this afternoon, and this one under discussion is a very large and a very important item. Let me also remind my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Brown) that I do not recall a day last session or this

Well, I imagine

Having made my protest
against listening to the same statement over and over again I will withdraw any specific objection I offered.

My difficulty is
to refuse a request made in such a gentlemanly way.
Do not refuse it.

Could it not be arranged
that on some other item anyone who is out of the House to-night might express his opinions on live stock? I noticed to-night that matters which had no bearing whatever upon live stock were discussed here.

Let us go on for another
hour.

I have no serious objections, provided hon. members on this side be given that opportunity, and that the arrangement be clearly understood.

Just before we close I would like a little information. I have spoken about duplication of effort on the part of the federal government and the provincial government. At the same summer fair last year I saw the federal government in charge of a live stock exhibition and the provincial government in charge of a live stock exhibition. I would like to know how many bulls were sold under this live stock distribution, what the cost of the bulls was and what the expenses were.

You mean loaned,
not sold?

No; I am asking how many
were sold and what expenses were incurred- that is, in the live stock promotion and in the distribution of animals.

We do not sell any of them except the old ones. Altogether something like 1,500 are loaned to the cattle clubs throughout the Dominion Last year alone 301 new ones were loaned. The cost was $42,571, an average of $141 for each animal.

The cost of distribution is
what I am after.
That would be difficult to secure; to get the cost per animal would require a good deal of accounting.
What was the total cost?

I find that in Saskatchewan alone we have Mr. Byers with a salary of $1,646, a bonus of $54 and an expense account of $2,770. Mr. Byers is a stock promoter. These men are not all engaged in the distribution.

Well, animals will
